video_title: Are Higher Rates Worse Than ZIRP? | Animal Spirits 486
gist: Ben Carlson and Michael Batnick revisit AI concentration, capex and bubble risk (top five stocks equal the bottom 434, memory stocks down about 32%), debate whether higher rates are worse than ZIRP given frozen housing, and cover tariffs, survey-data caveats, Kalshi long-shot betting and pop culture.

insights.claim: Since January 2024, AI stocks account for about two-thirds of S&P price return, 60% of earnings growth and 81% of capex, per charts from Michael Semblast.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Concentration is backed by fundamentals, not just price.
insights.quote: twothirds of the price return, 60% of earnings growth, and 81% of capex

insights.claim: The top five S&P 500 stocks equaled the bottom 282 companies in July 2018 and now equal the bottom 434 (stocks ranked about 67 through 500); trailing 12-month net income of the top five also roughly equals the bottom 436.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Profit share tracks market-cap share, so concentration reflects earnings power and is not a pure valuation distortion.
insights.quote: the top five stocks are now equal to the bottom 434.

insights.claim: Broad market breadth (many stocks beating the index) tends to show up in bear markets, as in 2001, so wishing for parity in the market is the wrong wish.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Narrow leadership is a feature of the modern bull market, not by itself a bear signal.
insights.quote: Be careful what you wish for.

insights.claim: Concentration is the natural-monopoly outcome of the last 15 years, has been called a risk for a decade (Apple at $1 trillion in 2018, Galloway's The Four), and is fine until it is not; the hosts note breakup risk faded because government and consumers do not want it.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Regulatory breakup is not a near-term catalyst for the megacaps.

insights.claim: In 2026 year-to-date small caps (Russell 2000 up about 15%) are outperforming the S&P (up about 12-13%); equal weight is up almost 13% and mid caps almost 12%, so the rest of the market is also doing fine despite narrow-breadth narratives.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The concentration worry is not matched by weak non-megacap returns this year.

insights.claim: A concentration hedge is simple: buy bonds (if AI stops, inflation and rates fall), European equities (little big tech and the dollar would fall), REITs and rate-sensitive, value, quality and dividend payers.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete portfolio hedge for an AI unwind built from rate, dollar and sector exposures.
insights.quote: if you want to hedge the concentration risk, it's easy.

insights.claim: Large AI companies' net interest cost as a share of profits has kept falling while the Fed funds rate rose, because they locked in low rates and profits grew, so higher rates have not hurt them.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Higher-for-longer rates mostly bite smaller and refinancing borrowers, not megacap tech.

insights.claim: The claim that growth stocks only worked because of ZIRP was true for weak growth names, but most growth stocks actually grew into their valuations after rates rose.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Rate sensitivity of quality growth was overstated.

themes.theme: AI capex, bubble risk and adoption

insights.claim: Zuckerberg and Alexander Wang describing Meta's AI build-out implied there is no dipping a toe in: the spending must work or it is a hard landing, so there is no soft-landing scenario for AI capex.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: AI risk is binary, which supports tail-risk thinking about hyperscaler capex.
insights.quote: This is either it has to work or there's a hard landing.

insights.claim: Michael expects a roughly 30% swift bear market at some point from an AI hiccup, which would be an unbelievable buying opportunity because AI will still deliver; Ben says a hard landing would be sharp but unlike the dotcom 12-year bear it would be quick, though trillions could be burned.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A fast drawdown is the base case of these hosts, with the long-term AI thesis intact.

insights.claim: Real construction spending year over year shows data centers up 65% while nearly every other category, including manufacturing (down about 24%), housing, offices and healthcare, is down, so AI is propping up the economy while crowding out other building.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The construction economy is a one-trade story, and an AI capex pause would hit with no replacement.

insights.claim: Memory-chip stocks fell about 32-35% in a short span: the DRAM ETF is down 32% (still about $23 billion in assets) and Western Digital was cut in half, with SanDisk, Micron and Seagate also hit.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Momentum in AI hardware is cracking sharply, and the corrections are fast.

insights.claim: Only about 2% of households pay for AI versus 12.6% that rent a storage unit, a contrast for how early AI consumer monetization is.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Large room for AI consumer adoption, and a reminder of how little revenue exists against capex.
insights.quote: 2% of households pay for AI. 12.6% of households have a storage unit.

insights.claim: Per Torsten Slok using Microsoft data, European countries (Norway, Ireland, France, Spain, UK, Netherlands) are ahead of the US in consumer generative AI adoption among 15-to-64-year-olds, supporting the idea that AI lets the rest of the world catch up without having to invest.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: AI could narrow the US edge over countries that did not bear the capex.

insights.claim: Agentic AI shopping may be overblown because people enjoy shopping and get a dopamine hit from it, citing Stitch Fix's collapse to $2.75 as evidence of a pandemic-era story that did not last.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of agent-commerce displacing consumer browsing.

insights.claim: For public commentators the rational stance on AI is optimism, because doom predictions earn nothing if right and make you unserious if the world does not end.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Explains the structural optimism bias among AI commentators.

insights.claim: Practical AI use cases cited: a deck builder records client conversations, has ChatGPT write the recap and a proposal from past proposals that is about 90% right, and wins by sending first; Michael used Claude to write a Google Docs script that clears the show doc.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Real small-business productivity gains come from speed-to-proposal and workflow glue rather than headline automation.

insights.claim: Michael argues current higher interest rates are worse for the US economy than ZIRP was in the 2010s, because ZIRP caused no real crisis whereas high rates have already helped crash housing activity, which is about 20% of the economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Challenges the consensus that zero rates were the larger policy mistake.
insights.quote: I think you could say that right now higher interest rates are worse than Zerp was for the economy.

insights.claim: Ben pushes back but concedes that for the current economy, rates around 2-3% would be better than 4-5%, and asks what imbalances ZIRP caused that led to a crisis.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Even skeptics see the current rate level as a drag.

insights.claim: Michael rejects the claim that ZIRP caused wealth inequality and populism, saying the system causes inequality and any rate regime can be blamed for it.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Counters a common macro narrative linking easy money to populism.

insights.claim: US existing home sales adjusted per 10,000 residents (population 280 million in 2000, over 343 million now) have sat at GFC-bottom levels for three years, worse than the GFC in duration; homebuilders like KB Home, Pulte and Lennar are making new multi-year lows as incentives stop working.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Housing remains frozen by rates and the lock-in effect, and builders are losing their subsidy-driven edge.

themes.theme: Tariffs, wealth data and the economy

insights.claim: A New York Fed report says tariffs contributed 2.9 percentage points to goods price inflation by February 2026; the hosts note manufacturing fell and the promised manufacturing revival did not happen, calling tariffs one of the worst economic ideas with no tangible benefit.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Tariffs added a measurable inflation tax without a manufacturing offset.
insights.quote: by February 2026, tariffs had contributed 2.9 percentage points to the goods price inflation.

insights.claim: The Fed's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances shows real median net worth up 35% for those 75 and older and down over 20% for those 35 and under since 2022, but response rates have dropped (general population from 65% to 45%, wealthy from 33% to 24%), so the survey likely under-reports national wealth.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Read headline generational-wealth survey results with caution; tax-return based data is better.
insights.quote: rich people are no longer answering surveys and do so at a much lower rate.

insights.claim: Since 2019 the under-35 median net worth is up almost 90% after inflation, the biggest increase, and Nick Maggiulli's data shows median net worth of young renters under 35 rising from about $5,000 to $12,000, so young people are financially okay with 4% unemployment even though they are mentally and socially struggling.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The financial 'young people are screwed' narrative is overstated.

insights.claim: Egan-Jones data shows China and Japan are outliers: China's economic growth and wages (up 13x versus 2.2x for the US from 2000 to 2024) had no relationship to its financial market performance, so the two other biggest economies cannot be used to test economic theory.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Growth does not equal equity returns; the largest comparators are unusable for macro lessons.

insights.claim: On Kalshi, since the start of 2025 half of trading volume has been on bets chasing returns of at least 1,000% (about 65% of that in sports parlays), and 41% of contracts involved outcomes with under 10% probability; 12% of Polymarket contracts bet against a 90%+ favorite.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Prediction markets are used as long-shot lotteries rather than hedges, raising the odds of regulatory backlash.

insights.claim: Single-stock options volume has returned to 2021 mania levels after crashing, showing retail speculators did not go away.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Retail speculation is again at peak-era intensity, a froth signal.

insights.claim: A shoe-shine style anecdote: a young man in an airport said he sold stocks to pay for concerts and mentioned that things would be a problem if the stock market stops going up.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Anecdotal sign that retail views the market as a one-way ATM.

insights.claim: Ray Dalio's line that bubbles pop when people have to sell to spend paper wealth is dismissed by the hosts, who ask what would force rich people to sell, apart from boomers selling 401(k) assets.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Skeptical of Dalio's forced-selling mechanism for a bubble pop.

insights.claim: Higher earners are no longer maxing out 401(k)s, preferring brokerage accounts for flexibility and early retirement, though the hosts argue retirement accounts keep investors disciplined and out of trouble.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Behavior-based argument for keeping money in locked-away accounts.

insights.claim: Alcohol consumption is at the lowest in US history and young people are less social and more risk-averse because of phones and surveillance anxiety (Derek Thompson interview with Daniel Cox), such as empty dance floors.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Consumer-staples and nightlife demand faces a structural generational headwind.

insights.claim: Nike is being demolished, with Jordan Brand down mid-teens year over year and the stock down nearly every day this year.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Continued weakness in a once-premium consumer brand.

insights.claim: Disney is raising prices on premium products (skip-the-line near $500) while holding entry-level prices, a way of capturing wealthier customers.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Pricing power is concentrated at the top of the income distribution.

insights.claim: Paramount's roughly $52 billion debt deal for Warner Brothers was oversubscribed but would have saved about $400 million in annual interest had it been done four months earlier; Ben says it will not work for equity holders given no media deal with that debt load has paid off.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Bearish on equity returns of leveraged media mergers.

insights.claim: Rotten Tomatoes critic scores have inflated, with the average rising from 57 in 2003 to 72 now, so Spielberg's flat scores obscure his box office duds.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Critic-score metrics are an unreliable signal.
